name: Cost per serving
description: Divides the total cost by the number of servings to find how much each serving costs. Useful for budgeting recipes or meal planning.
notes: Servings must be a positive count; the result is cost per one serving. Include all ingredient costs in the total for an accurate figure.

name: Recipe scaling
description: Scales an ingredient amount for a new number of servings using amount × new servings / original servings. It keeps ingredient proportions the same as the original recipe.
notes: Assumes ingredients scale linearly, which is a good approximation but may not hold for seasonings, leavening, or cooking times.

name: Oven temp C to gas mark
description: Converts an oven temperature in Celsius to the British gas mark scale using (temp − 121) / 14. Higher gas marks correspond to hotter ovens.
notes: This is a linear approximation of the standard gas-mark table and may give fractional marks; round to the nearest whole mark in practice. Valid mainly within typical baking temperatures.

name: Cooking time by weight
description: Estimates total cooking time by multiplying the minutes required per kilogram by the weight of the food.
notes: The per-kilogram rate depends on the dish, oven, and doneness desired. Use a thermometer to confirm safe internal temperature rather than relying on time alone.

name: Coffee dose from water ratio
description: Divides the amount of water by the water-to-coffee ratio to find how many grams of ground coffee to use. A higher ratio means more water per gram of coffee and a weaker brew.
notes: The ratio is dimensionless (water grams per coffee gram); a value of 16 means 16 g water to 1 g coffee. Water is entered by weight in grams, where 1 g water is about 1 mL.

name: Sterilisation Value F₀
description: Adds up the lethality of a heat process as equivalent minutes at 121.1 °C, the standard for canned foods (F₀ ≥ 3 min for botulinum safety).
notes: Each 10 K below 121.1 °C counts ten times less.

name: Time for a Log Reduction (D-Value)
description: Gives the heating time for a chosen microbial reduction: each D-value kills 90 %.
notes: The botulinum "12D" process reduces spores by a factor of 10¹².

name: Pasteurisation Units
description: Gives the heat treatment of beer and juice in pasteurisation units: one minute at 60 °C is 1 PU (z ≈ 7 K).
notes: Beer is typically given 15–25 PU.

name: Baker's Percentage
description: Computes the weight of an ingredient as a percentage of the total flour weight, the standard way bakers write recipes.
notes: The flour is always 100 %. For water, the result is the dough hydration.

name: Brine Concentration
description: Computes the salt concentration of a brine as salt weight divided by the total weight of salt and water.
notes: This is a percentage by weight of the whole brine. Some recipes instead give salt as a percentage of the water alone.

name: Salt for a Target Brine Strength
description: Computes the salt to dissolve in a given weight of water to make a brine of the target concentration by weight.
notes: The concentration is salt as a share of the total brine (salt + water). 1 L of water weighs about 1000 g.

name: Raw Weight Needed for a Cooked Portion
description: Computes how much raw food to buy for a cooked weight, from the cooking yield (cooked weight as a percentage of raw weight).
notes: Meat often loses 20–35 % of its weight in cooking; dry rice and pasta gain weight, so their yield is above 100 %.

name: Menu Price from a Target Food Cost
description: Computes the selling price at which the ingredient cost of a dish is the target percentage of the price.
notes: Restaurants commonly aim for a food cost of about 25–35 %. Tax is not included.

name: Share of Energy from Protein
description: Computes the percentage of a food's energy that comes from protein, using the Atwater factor of 4 kcal per gram.
notes: The same method gives the share from carbohydrate (4 kcal/g) or fat (9 kcal/g) when those factors are used instead.

name: Coffee Extraction Yield
description: Computes the percentage of the ground coffee's weight that dissolved into the drink, from the measured TDS and the weights.
notes: TDS is measured with a refractometer. Brewed coffee is commonly aimed at an extraction of about 18–22 %.

name: Alcohol by Volume from Gravity Readings
description: Estimates the alcohol content of beer or wine from the specific gravity before and after fermentation, using the common homebrewing factor 131.25.
notes: This simple formula is an approximation that is good for normal-strength beer; it underestimates strong beers and wines.

name: Recipe Scaling for a Round Pan Size
description: Scales an ingredient amount for a round pan of a different diameter, keeping the same depth of batter.
notes: The amount grows with the pan area, so with the square of the diameter: a 24 cm pan needs 1.44 times a 20 cm pan.

name: Recipe Scaling from a Rectangular to a Round Pan
description: Scales an ingredient amount from a rectangular pan to a round pan by the ratio of their base areas.
notes: The batter depth stays the same. Baking time may need to change with the new shape.

name: US Standard Drinks
description: Computes the number of US standard drinks in a drink; one US standard drink contains 14 g of pure alcohol.
notes: Uses an alcohol density of 0.789 g/mL. Other countries define the standard drink differently (for example 10 g in Australia).

name: Water Temperature for a Target Dough Temperature
description: Computes the water temperature needed for a straight dough to reach the desired temperature after mixing, by the bakers' three-factor method.
notes: The friction factor is the heat added by the mixer and depends on the machine and mixing time; a pre-ferment adds a fourth term.

name: Sugar Concentration after Dilution
description: Computes the sugar concentration (degrees Brix, grams of sugar per 100 g) of a syrup or juice after water is added.
notes: Brix is a percentage by weight, so the weights, not the volumes, of syrup and water are used.

name: Pearson Square: Amount of the Richer Ingredient
description: Computes how much of the richer of two ingredients to mix with the leaner one to reach a target content, for example cream and milk for a target fat percentage.
notes: The rest of the total is the leaner ingredient. The target must lie between the two contents.

name: Sourdough Hydration Including the Starter
description: Computes the overall hydration of a sourdough, counting the flour and water that are inside the starter.
notes: A starter at 100 % hydration is half flour and half water by weight.

name: Alcohol Content of a Mixed Drink
description: Computes the alcohol by volume of a mixed drink from the spirit, a non-alcoholic mixer and the water added by melting ice.
notes: Dilution is the melted water as a percentage of the drink before it is stirred or shaken; it is often about 20–30 %. Volume shrinkage on mixing is ignored.
